Differential protein abundance analysis (Joan Chang, Liz Laird)

Fraction 2 - data processing and statistical inference

Introduction

This report details the analysis pipeline for this proteomic study, which includes data processing steps to filter and normalize the peptide data, unsupervised exploratory analyses such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA) and hierarchical clustering, and statistical analyses to identify differentially expressed proteins.

For the comparative analysis, we used the msqrob2 package, which implements a robust linear (mixed) model framework for differential abundance testing. Briefly, a model is fitted per protein, with the experimental design specified as a formula; fixed and random effects can be included, so that nested designs, batch structure and technical replication are modelled explicitly rather than collapsed into a two-sample test. Parameter estimates are stabilised by three mechanisms: robust M-estimation, which down-weights outliers rather than discarding them; ridge regression, which shrinks coefficients and stabilises estimation when a protein is quantified by few or unbalanced peptides; and empirical Bayes moderation of the residual variance, which borrows information across proteins to improve variance estimates in small-sample designs. Contrasts of interest are then tested using moderated t-statistics, and p-values are corrected for multiple testing across proteins with using Benjamini–Hochberg correction.

Input data

The MS/MS data was searched against the mouse proteome, obtained from UniProtKB (Proteome UP000000589, downloaded on 03/08/2026; containing 54,857 protein sequences) using FragPipe’s integrated search algorithm MSFragger. The search generates a combined_peptide.tsv, which contains 1% FDR-filtered peptides from all experimental groups, where each row is a (stripped) peptide sequence, and their respective normalized intensities.

Briefly, the search was performed with the following settings:

  • Precursor mass tolerance: 20 ppm (window is +/- this value)
  • Fragment mass tolerance: 20 ppm
  • Protease: Trypsin, with 2 missed cleavages allowed per peptide
  • Fixed modifications: carbamidomethylation of cysteine (+57.02146 Da)
  • Variable modifications: oxidation of methionine (+15.9949 Da), N-terminal acetylation (+42.0106 Da)
  • Peptide length: 7 to 50 residues
  • Precursor mass tolerance: 500 to 5000 Da

A target-decoy search strategy was applied to control for false-positive identifications, maintaining a 1% FDR for both peptide-spectrum matches and protein groups. The match-between-runs algorithm was enabled during the analysis to increase the number of identifications. Contaminants were identified based on matches to the contaminants database.

Code 
# Load the peptide data
peptides = "combined_peptide.tsv" # use the combined peptide as input data

peptide_data = data.table::fread(peptides, check.names = TRUE,
                                 integer64 = "double", sep = "\t")

# Remove the peptides that map to decoy sequences or to contaminants proteins
peptide_data = peptide_data[!grepl("contam_|rev_", peptide_data$Protein), ]

# Locate expression variables in the peptide table
quantCols = grep("\\d+.Intensity", names(peptide_data), value = TRUE)

# Identify pooled samples (if present) and remove it
if(any(grepl("pool", names(peptides[quantCols]), ignore.case = TRUE))) {
  quantCols <- quantCols[!grepl("pool", names(peptides[quantCols]), ignore.case = TRUE)]
  }

Metadata table detailing study design

Sample annotations were retrieved from the experiment_annotation.tsv that shows the group labels set for the data search with FragPipe. This dataset comprises four groups which were searched together:

  • Group A: C57BL6/J; Wt for oim
  • Group B: oim/oim homozgyote on C57BL6/J
  • Group C: C57BL6N; Wt for Col1a2 null
  • Group D: Col1a2 null (-/-) (tm1b) on C57BL6N

Comparisons will be performed as:

  • Group B vs. Group A
  • Group C vs. Group A
  • Group D vs. Group C
  • Group D vs. Group B
Code 
annot = data.frame(quantCols = quantCols)
annot = annot |> 
  dplyr::mutate(
    SampleId = gsub(".Intensity", "", quantCols),
    condition = gsub("_\\d+.Intensity", "", quantCols),
    Replicate = rep(1:3, 4)
  )

Convert to QFeatures object

For this pipeline, we use the peptide data table to generate a QFeatures object so we can directly use QFeatures’ data preprocessing functionality. QFeatures allows to build highly modular workflows, where each step is carried out by a dedicated function with a large choice of available methods and parameters, which lets the users to adapt the workflow to their specific use case and their specific needs.

We use the readQFeatures() from the QFeatures package, which converts a tabular data into a QFeatures object. We provide the peptide table and the sample annotation table. The function will use the quantCols column in the sample annotation table to understand which columns in peptides contain the quantitative values, and automatically link the corresponding sample annotation with the quantitative values. We also tell the function to use the Sequence column as peptide identifier, which will be used as row names.

Following, we apply a function to correctly encode the missing values because it is important that missing values are encoded using NA. For instance, non-observed values should not be encoded with a zero because true zeros (the proteomic feature is absent from the sample) cannot be distinguished from technical zeros (the feature was missed by the instrument or could not be identified). We therefore replace any zero in the quantitative data with NA.

Next, we log2-transform the peptide intensities to mitigate the impact of highly variable peptide intensities and enhances the comparability of the data. This step is essential for downstream statistical analyses, which often assume normally distributed data. Furthermore, with this transformation, we can visually inspect the data distribution to identify discrete variations in peptide signal distribution among replicates, with some noise, and whether there is a necessity for normalization.

Code 
# Create an S4 object, QFeatures type
pep = 
  QFeatures::readQFeatures(
    assayData = peptide_data,    # quantitative peptide data
    colData = annot,             # metadata
    quantCols = quantCols,       # expression indexes: using IonQuant Intensities here
    fnames = "Peptide.Sequence", # feature names
    name = "raw",                # assay name
    sep = "\t"
  )

# Convert zeroes to NA
pep = QFeatures::zeroIsNA(object = pep, i = "raw")

# log2-transformation
pep = QFeatures::logTransform(pep, base = 2, i = "raw", name = "log")
Code 
# Brief summary
cat(paste("The dataset contains",
          nrow(assay(pep[["log"]])), "peptide sequences and",
          ncol(assay(pep[["log"]])), "samples")
    )
The dataset contains 11211 peptide sequences and 12 samples

QC: missing values

Missing MS signal values is a common feature in discovery proteomics, and can influence the robustness of further analyses. Mass spectrometry does not measure every protein in every sample. Because the instrument selects peptides for fragmentation semi-randomly, and because low-abundance peptides fall below the detection limit in some runs but not others, the final data table contains a substantial number of empty cells. These gaps carry information that provide insights into patterns and biases within the dataset, and ultimately constrains which proteins can be tested statistically.

Examining the distribution and prevalence of missing MS values helps identify patterns and potential biases in the dataset, which should be handled properly during data wrangling so the results of the later analyses are robust and reliable. Overall, missing values should be randomly distributed across the replicates, and if not, that could indicate systematic issues that need to be addressed.

Code 
MSnbase::plotNA(assay(pep[["log"]]))

In Figure 1, features are sorted from the most to the least completely measured, and two quantities plotted. The cyan step line shows how completely each individual feature was measured: those on the left were detected in all 6 samples, those on the right in only one or two. The smooth red line shows the cumulative effect of filtering, that is, how complete the data table would be if only the best-measured features on its left were retained. For this dataset, 11,211 peptides is 40% complete, meaning 60% of all possible measurements are missing. However, this missingness is very unevenly distributed: 4,038 features (~36% of the total) were measured in at least half of the samples, and this subset is 73% complete. In other words, most of the missing values are concentrated in a minority of poorly detected features. Notably, the missingness is consistent across samples and decreases monotonically as progressively sparser features are added.

Preprocessing

Here, the peptide data is submitted to a series of filtering steps aimed to enhance the quality of the peptide data and appropriate normalization to remove systematic biases to prepare it for subsequent analyses.

Peptide filtering

Filtering steps will remove peptides not-suitable for analysis. These include peptides that failed during protein inference, or matching to contaminant proteins and reverse sequences (decoys) or to multiple smaller protein groups, and peptides detected in only one sample. This rigorous filtering ensures that only high-confidence peptides are considered for the analysis.

Code 
# failed protein inference (if any)
prot = rowData(pep[["log"]])$Protein
rowData(pep[["log"]])$has_protein = !is.na(prot) & trimws(prot) != ""
#sum(!rowData(pep[["log"]])$has_protein)          # report this; likely 0
pep = QFeatures::filterFeatures(pep, ~ has_protein, keep = TRUE)

# gene-level uniquenes
mg = rowData(pep[["log"]])$Mapped.Genes
rowData(pep[["log"]])$gene_unique = is.na(mg) | trimws(mg) == ""
#table(rowData(pep[["log"]])$gene_unique)
pep = QFeatures::filterFeatures(pep, ~ gene_unique, keep = TRUE)

# remove peptides with high missingness rates: add column with count of non-zero values to assay array
# keep peptides that were detected in at least two samples, for modelling of peptide characteristics later with msqrob2
rowData(pep[["log"]])$nNonZero = rowSums(!is.na(assay(pep[["log"]])))
pep = QFeatures::filterFeatures(pep, ~ nNonZero > 1, keep = TRUE)

cat(paste("Before filtering, the dataset comprised a total of",
      nrow(assay(pep[["raw"]])), "peptide sequences. After filtering was performed, it now comprises",
      nrow(assay(pep[["log"]])), "peptide sequences."))
Before filtering, the dataset comprised a total of 11211 peptide sequences. After filtering was performed, it now comprises 7818 peptide sequences.

After filtering was applied, we can inspect various peptide measurements. Figure 2 illustrates the total peptide signal detected and missed in each replicate sample within the respective samples. These measurements facilitate the assessment of variability between replicates and the overall quality of the data

Peptide normalization

The most common objective of MS-based proteomics experiments is to understand the biological changes in protein abundance between experimental conditions. However, changes in measurements between groups can be caused due to technical factors such as differences in sample preparation or instrument performance. Normalization corrects for these systematic biases and variability between samples, ensuring that differences observed in the data are due to biological variation rather than technical artefacts.

Figure 3 shows the distribution of the log2-transformed peptide intensities across each replicate prior to normalization. We use this to diagnose the need for normalization to account for technical variability between replicates.

Code 
hist1 = 
  ggplot(reshape2::melt(assay(pep[["log"]]))) +
  geom_density(aes(x = value,
                   color = gsub(".Intensity", "", Var2))) +
  xlab("Log2-peptide intensity") + ylab("Density") +
  labs(color = "", tag = "A") +
  theme_linedraw() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "black"),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12, color = "black"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 12)
        )

bp1 = 
  ggplot(reshape2::melt(assay(pep[["log"]]))) +
  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Var2, y = value,
                   fill = gsub(".Intensity", "", Var2))) +
  ylab("Log2-peptide intensity") + xlab("") +
  labs(fill = "", tag = "B") +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_blank(),
        axis.text.y = element_text(size = 10, color = "black"),
        axis.ticks = element_blank(),
        axis.title = element_text(size = 12, color = "black"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 12)
        )

hist1+bp1

Both the histogram (A) and box plot (B) reveal notable variations in peptide signal distribution among all replicates, both within and across groups. Note that the marginal precursor intensity distributions across samples are not well aligned. Ignoring this effect will increase the noise and reduce the statistical power of the experiment, and may also, in case of unbalanced designs, introduce confounding effects that will bias the results.

There are many ways to perform the normalisation, e.g. median centring is a popular choice. If we subtract the sample median at the log scale from each precursor log2 intensity, centring the data around zero - this basically boils down to calculating log-ratios between the precursor intensity and its sample median. For this, we use a matrix containing peptide intensity values to apply median centring, which will help to reduce technical variability and improve the comparability of samples. Figure 4 shows the distribution of the peptide intensities per sample, before and after normalization

Code 
# Apply median centring
pep = QFeatures::normalize(pep, i = "log", method = "center.median", name = "norm")

  geom_density(aes(x = value,

  labs(color = "", tag = "C") +
  theme_linedraw() +

        axis.title = element_text(size = 12, color = "black"),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10),
        plot.tag = element_text(size = 12)
        )

bp2 =

  geom_boxplot(aes(x = Var2, y = value,

Principal Component Analysis

The next step involves investigating the sources of variation in the data and identifying potential outliers that will need to be addressed before conducting statistical analyses. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) identifies variation patterns in the data and simplifies the dataset by reducing the number of variables while retaining the majority of its essential information. The initial step involves calculating the overall rate of missing values in the dataset.

Missing values, if random, typically do not significantly affect PCA unless they are excessively prevalent. It is advisable to filter features with a high rate of missing values and impute the remaining missing values. Proteins with an excessive number of missing values should be excluded to maintain the accuracy of the principal components calculation. Typically, a 20-30% threshold is applied to the data to determine whether variables with an excessive number of missing values should be removed. If this assumption is not met, variables with excessive missing values should be removed to maintain the precision of the principal components’ calculation.

Code 
prop.na = function(df){
  num.NA = sum(is.na(dplyr::select_if(df, is.numeric)))
  num.nNA = sum(!is.na(dplyr::select_if(df, is.numeric)))
  prop.na = 100*(num.NA/(num.nNA+num.NA))
  
  if(prop.na > 20){
    cat(paste("The proportion of missing values in the dataset exceeds 20%, the next step is to remove variables with an excessive number of missing values, specifically those that were not quantified in more than 20% of the samples."))
    
  } else{
    cat(paste("The proportion of missing values in the dataset at hand is less than 20%, hence, no filtering for variables with with an excessive number of missing values is required."))
  }
  }

prop.na(protein_data)
The proportion of missing values in the dataset exceeds 20%, the next step is to remove variables with an excessive number of missing values, specifically those that were not quantified in more than 20% of the samples.
Code 
remove_variables = function(df){
  # calculate NA rate per variable (proteins displayed in rows)
    df$prop.na = apply(select_if(df, is.numeric), 1, function(x) sum(is.na(x))/length(x))
  
  # remove variables with > 20% values missing  
    df = df |>
      dplyr::filter(prop.na < 0.2) |> 
      dplyr::select(!c(Protein, Gene, prop.na))
    }

protein_filtered = remove_variables(protein_data)

cat(paste("A total of", nrow(protein_data)-nrow(protein_filtered), 
          "proteins were removed from the original protein list, resulting in a filtered dataset containing", 
          nrow(protein_filtered), "proteins selected for further analysis using Principal Component Analysis."))
A total of 1120 proteins were removed from the original protein list, resulting in a filtered dataset containing 376 proteins selected for further analysis using Principal Component Analysis.

Missing values should be further imputed, and here, the NIPALS algorithm, from the mixOmics package is used to decompose the dataset and extract information used for reconstructing the original data. Estimated values replace the missing ones before proceeding with PCA.

Code 
# transpose the data
protein_t = 
  protein_filtered |>
  t()

# impute missing values with NIPALS
set.seed(123)
protein_t = mixOmics::impute.nipals(protein_t, ncomp = nrow(protein_t))

# Global adequacy for PCA
## Pearson correlation matrix
rcor = Hmisc::rcorr(protein_t)

## Bartlett's sphericity test
## if $p.value < 0.05, a PCA is adequate
#psych::cortest.bartlett(rcor$r, n = nrow(rcor$r)) # $p.value = 0
Code 
pca = mixOmics::pca(X = protein_t, ncomp = 3, center = TRUE, scale = FALSE)

To calculate the principal components, a factorial analysis is performed with the pca() function from the mixOmics package. Figure 7 depicts a sample plot where the samples are represented as points positioned according to their projections onto the first three principal components obtained through PCA. Points in these plots tend to cluster together when they share similarities.

Code 
plotIndiv(object = pca,
          comp = c(1,2),
          ind.names = FALSE,
          ellipse = TRUE,
          group = annot$condition,
          legend = TRUE,
          legend.title = "Group",
          title = "PCA"
          )

Statistical analysis

Protein intensities are tested for differential expression (DE) using the msqrob2 package. For the statistical testing, we only include the proteins present in more than 50% of the samples in each condition, that is n = 2 out of 3 samples for this study design. Requiring observation in all samples systematically discards low-abundance and genuinely condition-specific proteins, which are frequently the ones with the largest true effects.

Code 
rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naA = apply(assay(pep[["prot"]])[, 1:3],   1, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naB = apply(assay(pep[["prot"]])[, 4:6],   1, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
rowData(pep[["prot"]])$nac = apply(assay(pep[["prot"]])[, 7:9],   1, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))
rowData(pep[["prot"]])$nad = apply(assay(pep[["prot"]])[, 10:12], 1, function(x) sum(is.na(x)))

filter_prot = (rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naA < 2 & rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naB < 2 & rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naB < 2 & rowData(pep[["prot"]])$naB < 2)
pep[["prot"]] = pep[["prot"]][filter_prot, ]

We will not include values that were imputed because a fundamental problem with imputation is that imputed values are artificial, but are treated as equally certain as actually measured values by any downstream processing, which can invalidate inferential conclusions by underestimating statistical uncertainty or cause loss of power. msqrob2 doesn’t impute, but fits the peptide-level model on observed values only and lets the design matrix carry fewer observations for sparser peptides, with empirical Bayes variance moderation on top. Missingness reduces power for that protein, which is the correct behaviour.

Estimation and inference

Protein level expression summaries are tested for differential expression (DE) using the msqrob2 pipeline. By default, msqrob2 estimates the model parameters using robust regression, and then corrects the p-values for multiple testing using the Benjamini-Hochberg method to control the FDR.

Estimating the model: for this study, Group A serves as the reference condition, against which fold-changes will be calculated, and factor levels A, B, C, D, msqrob2 will parameterize the model as:

A = β0 B = β0 + βB C = β0 + βC D = β0 + βD

The fitted coefficients are:

  • (Intercept) = mean of A
  • GroupB = B - A
  • GroupC = C - A
  • GroupD = D - A
  • GroupD - groupC = (D - A) - (C - A) = D - C

These represent the average log2-fold change for Groups B-D vs. Group A. Therefore, the three contrasts we will use to generate null hypotheses for statistical testing

Code 
# create model for proteins
pep = msqrob(object = pep, i = "prot", formula = ~condition, robust = TRUE)
model = rowData(pep[["prot"]])[["msqrobModels"]]

For the inference, we translated the question into a null and alternative hypothesis on a single model parameter or on a linear combination of model parameters, which is also referred to with a contrast. To aid defining contrasts, we will visualise the experimental design using the ExploreModelMatrix package.

Code 
vd = 
  ExploreModelMatrix::VisualizeDesign(
    sampleData =  colData(pep),
    designFormula = ~condition,
    textSizeFitted = 4
    )

vd$plotlist
[[1]]

Based on this null hypothesis we now generate a contrast matrix to then test the null hypothesis using hypothesisTest() which takes the QFeatures object with the fitted model and the contrast we just built. msqrob2 automatically applies the hypothesis testing to all features in the assay.

Code 
# check condition name
msqrob2::getCoef(rowData(pep[["prot"]])$msqrobModels[[1]])
     (Intercept) conditionGroup_B conditionGroup_C conditionGroup_D 
       1.2328261       -2.7543317       -0.7674499       -0.8387862
Code 
# make contrast
contrast = 
  msqrob2::makeContrast(
    contrasts = c(
      "conditionGroup_B = 0",
      "conditionGroup_C = 0",
      "conditionGroup_D - conditionGroup_C = 0",
      "conditionGroup_D - conditionGroup_B = 0"
      ),
    parameterNames = 
      colnames(vd$designmatrix)
    )

# hypothesis test
pep = msqrob2::hypothesisTest(object = pep, i = "prot", contrast = contrast)

The results of the statistical testing can be inspected via the msqrobCollect() function from the msqrob2 package - this function automatically retrieves the results for all contrasts in one table that contains two additional columns: contrast with the name of the contrast and feature with the name of the modelled feature, here protein. These results are shown in Table 3.

Code 
# Extract comparison data
compData = msqrob2::msqrobCollect(pep[["prot"]], contrast = contrast)

# Reorganize compData
compData = 
  compData |> 
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(adjPval)) |> 
  dplyr::rename(Protein = "feature") |> 
  dplyr::left_join(protein_data, by = "Protein") |> 
  dplyr::relocate(Protein, Gene, contrast)

#write.xlsx(x = compData, file = "Comparison_results.xlsx")

compData |>
  DT::datatable(
    rownames = FALSE,
              extensions = 'Buttons', 
              options = list(dom = 'Bfrtip', buttons = 'excel'))


Volcano plots

A volcano plot is a common visualisation that provides an overview of the hypothesis testing results, plotting the −log(10)-P-value as a function of the estimated log(2)-fold change. Volcano plots can be used to highlight the most interesting proteins that have large fold changes and/or are highly significant.

To generate the volcano plot, by default we set some thresholds:

  • adjusted P-value < 0.05 (5%)
  • log2FC > 0.5 (corresponds to a 1.41-fold increase, or a 41% increase) or < -0.5 (correspond to a decrease greater than approximately 29.3%).

The proteins that pass these thresholds are highlighted in Figure 8 (Group B vs. Group A), Figure 9 (Group D vs. Group C), Figure 10 (Group D vs. Group B), and Figure 11 (Group C vs. Group A)

Code 
compData$label <- "Not-significant"
compData$label[compData$adjPval < 0.05 & compData$logFC > 0.5] <- "Up-regulated"
compData$label[compData$adjPval < 0.05 & compData$logFC < -0.5] <- "Down-regulated"

volcano_BA =
  compData |> 
  dplyr::filter(contrast == "conditionGroup_B") |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = logFC, y = -log(pval))) +
  geom_point(aes(color = label), size = 1) +
  labs(color = "") + 
  scale_color_manual(values = c("blue", "gray", "red")) +
  geom_text_repel(aes(label = 
                        ifelse(label == "Down-regulated"|label == "Up-regulated",
                               Gene, ""), max.overlaps = 30)) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "black"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "black"),
        panel.grid = element_blank(),
        legend.text = element_text(size = 10)
        )

volcano_DC =

  labs(color = "") +

  geom_text_repel(aes(label = 
                        ifelse(label == "Down-regulated"|label == "Up-regulated",
                               Gene, ""), max.overlaps = 30)) +
  theme_light() +
  theme(axis.text = element_text(size = 10, color = "black"),
        panel.border = element_rect(color = "black"),

        )

Heat map of proteins differentially abundant

We construct heat maps for the significant proteins for each comparison using the pheatmap package. We get the names of the significant features, extract the quantitative data for the significant features and scale it (via z-score transformation), and, optionally, perform hierarchical clustering (by default) on both rows and columns using Euclidean distance and complete linkage.

Figure 12 shows the heatmap for the proteins selected from the comparison between Group B and Group A.

Code 
#png(filename = "heatmap_BA.png", width = 12, height = 22, units = "cm", res = 600)
compData |> 
  dplyr::mutate(ID = paste0(Gene, "_", Protein)) |> 
  dplyr::filter(contrast == "conditionGroup_B") |> 
  dplyr::arrange(logFC) |> 
  dplyr::filter(adjPval < 0.05) |> 
  dplyr::filter(logFC > 0.5 | logFC < -0.5) |> 
  dplyr::select(10:15, ID) |> 
  column_to_rownames(var = "ID") |> 
  apply(1, zscore_custom) |> 
  t() |> 
  pheatmap(
    color = colorRampPalette(c("blue", "white", "red"))(50),
    na_col = "gray25",
    cluster_rows = T,
    cluster_cols = T,
    show_colnames = T,
    border_color = NA,
    fontsize = 6
    )
#dev.off()

Gene ontology and pathway enrichment analysis

Gene Ontology (GO) and pathway enrichment analyses are used in proteomics to identify biological processes, molecular functions, cellular components, and signalling or metabolic pathways that are overrepresented among proteins of interest. By comparing a selected protein list, such as differentially abundant proteins, with an appropriate background set of detected proteins, these analyses help translate protein-level changes into broader biological themes. They are therefore useful for generating hypotheses, identifying coordinated cellular responses, and interpreting the functional significance of proteomic datasets.

For this, we use the culsterProfiler package, which automates functional enrichment analysis and implements methods to analyze and visualize functional GO profiles of proteins and protein clusters. To perform the GO analysis, we select as background the set of proteins detected and eligible for statistical testing in the study (not the whole species-specific proteome, which will contain proteins that were never measurable in this experiment) because GO enrichment asks whether a category occurs more often than expected among your selected proteins, and the expectation must reflect the proteins that could realistically have entered that selected list.

GO enrichment analysis

For this study, we selected the 2356 proteins detected across the samples in the study. Next, we extract the proteins that were identified as up- and down-regulated based on the thresholds established before (i.e., adjusted p-value < 0.05, log(2)-fold change > 0.5 or < -0.5) and test them against the protein background.

Code 
# Define protein background (universe)
library(org.Mm.eg.db)

# Proteins to be tested
padj_cutoff = 0.05
lfc_cutoff  = 0.5

compData_clean = 
  compData |>
  dplyr::transmute(
    contrast = as.character(contrast),
    Protein     = as.character(Protein),
    logFC    = as.numeric(logFC),
    adjPval  = as.numeric(adjPval)
  ) |>
  dplyr::filter(
    !is.na(Protein),
    Protein != ""
    )

universe_symbols = 
  compData_clean |>
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(adjPval)) |>
  dplyr::pull(Protein) |>
  unique()

Figure 15 shows the top 20 GO terms enriched for the proteins significantly regulated from the comparison between Group B vs. Group A.

Code 
# Define significant up- and down-regulated proteins: Group B vs. Group A
up = 
  compData_clean |>
  dplyr::filter(
    contrast == "conditionGroup_B",
    !is.na(adjPval),
    adjPval < padj_cutoff,
    logFC > lfc_cutoff
    ) |>
  dplyr::pull(Protein) |>
  unique()

down = 
  compData_clean |>
  dplyr::filter(
    contrast == "conditionGroup_B",
    !is.na(adjPval),
    adjPval < padj_cutoff,
    logFC < lfc_cutoff
    ) |>
  dplyr::pull(Protein) |>
  unique()

combined = 
  c(up, down) |> 
  unlist() |> 
  unique()

gene_lists =
  list(
    Upregulated   = up,
    Downregulated = down,
    Combined      = combined
    )

# GO enrichment analysis
stopifnot(
  all(up %in% universe_symbols),
  all(down %in% universe_symbols)
  )

run_go = function(ontology) {
  clusterProfiler::compareCluster(
    geneCluster   = gene_lists,
    fun           = "enrichGO",
    universe      = universe_symbols,
    OrgDb         = org.Mm.eg.db,
    keyType       = "UNIPROT",
    ont           = ontology,
    pAdjustMethod = "fdr",
    pvalueCutoff  = 0.05,
    qvalueCutoff  = 0.10,
    minGSSize     = 2,
    maxGSSize     = 500,
    readable      = TRUE
  )
  }

go_results = 
  run_go("all") |> 
  clusterProfiler::simplify()

# filter explicitly by adjusted p-value
go_table_BA =
  as.data.frame(go_results) |> 
  dplyr::filter(p.adjust < 0.10) |>
  dplyr::arrange(p.adjust) |> 
  dplyr::mutate(comparison = "Group B vs. Group A")
Code 
plot_GO_BA = 
  enrichplot::dotplot(
    go_results,
    showCategory = 20
    ) +
  ggplot2::ggtitle("Gene ontology enrichment")

plot_GO_BA
